title: Horus: The Falcon Who Is Far Above
summary: A month with Heru, the falcon of the sky, the son who avenged his father and the living god of every king. Study his many forms, the long contest with Set, the Eye that was torn and made whole, and his temple at Edfu, keep ten mornings under the open sky, and decide whether to dedicate.
welcome:
This journey spends about a lunar month with Horus, the Egyptian falcon god of the sky and of rightful rule. He suits people who have had to stand up for themselves or for someone else, people rebuilding after an injury or a loss, people who carry responsibility for others, and anyone who wants courage that stays fair.

You will learn how many gods were called Horus and how they came together, the myth of his birth in the marshes and his long contest with Set for his father's throne, the Eye of Horus and what it really meant, and how he was served at Edfu and by every king of Egypt. For ten mornings you will greet him under the open sky. At the end you may dedicate yourself to him, or not.

This is a self-dedication. It is not an initiation into Kemetic Orthodoxy or any other temple or group, and it does not replace one. It has nothing to do with the "Aeon of Horus" of modern occultism, which this journey explains only so that you can tell the two apart.
about: Horus (Egyptian Heru, often written Hor) was the falcon god of the sky, whose eyes were the sun and the moon, and the god of kingship: from the very first dynasties the king was "the Horus", the god living on earth. The name covers several gods who merged over time. Horus the Elder (Heru-wer) was a sky falcon and, in the Heliopolitan family, a brother of Osiris; Horus son of Isis (Heru-sa-Aset, Greek Harsiesis) was the child conceived after Osiris's death, hidden in the Delta marshes, who grew up to defeat Set and take the throne; Horus the Child (Heru-pa-khered, Greek Harpocrates) was the infant on his mother's lap; Ra-Horakhty, "Ra who is Horus of the two horizons", joined him to the sun; and Horus of Behdet was the winged sun disc spread over temple doorways. His great cult centres were Nekhen (Hierakonpolis) in the far south, among the oldest sacred places in Egypt, and Edfu, where his Ptolemaic temple still stands almost complete. Today he is honoured in Kemetic religion, by reconstructionists and in Kemetic Orthodoxy, and by many modern Pagans as a god of protection, courage and right rule.
notes: "Horus" names several gods. Egyptians themselves blended and distinguished them by place and period. When you pray, it helps to know which form you mean: the sky falcon, the son of Isis, the child, the sun of the horizons or the winged disc.

The Contendings of Horus and Set, the longest telling of their quarrel, is a New Kingdom story with comic and crude episodes. It is one telling among many, not scripture, and Egyptians did not read it as a simple fight of good against evil.

The idea that the parts of the Eye of Horus stood for fractions (1/2, 1/4 and so on) is an early twentieth-century theory that most Egyptologists now doubt. The Eye as a sign of wholeness, healing and offering is well attested.
The "Aeon of Horus" belongs to Thelema, the religion founded by Aleister Crowley after 1904. It is a modern Western esoteric idea, not Egyptian religion; be clear which one you are working in.

Many falcons were mummified as offerings in antiquity. Do not buy animal mummies or other antiquities. Birds of prey are protected in most countries: never take a feather, nest or bird from the wild, and keep or fly a falcon only through licensed falconry.
Safety: keep incense smoke away from pet birds, and never look directly at the sun, even at sunrise.

stages.title: Under the Open Sky
stages.intro: Begin by learning who Horus is and making a shrine where you can see the sky. The threshold ends with a short introduction rite: you greet him by name and give him water, bread and incense.

lessons.title: Heru, the Distant One
lessons.summary: His name, his falcon, his many forms, and why every king was called Horus.

sections.heading: The falcon high up
sections.body:
His Egyptian name was Heru, which Egyptologists often connect with a word for "far above" or "the distant one". Whether that is the true origin is not certain, but it fits the bird. The falcon hangs high in the sky over the river and the desert edge, sees everything below, and drops like a stone. Egyptians watched it and saw a god.

He is shown as a falcon, often wearing the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt, or as a man with a falcon's head. The markings under a falcon's eye, the dark "tear" line, became the lines of the wedjat eye that you will meet later in this journey. His right eye was the sun and his left eye the moon, so the sky itself was his face.

sections.heading: Many gods called Horus
sections.body:
There was not one Horus but several, and Egyptians blended them freely. Horus the Elder, Heru-wer (Greek Haroeris), was the great sky falcon, honoured at places like Qus and Kom Ombo, and in the Heliopolitan family a brother of Osiris, Isis, Set and Nephthys. Horus son of Isis, Heru-sa-Aset, was the child of Osiris and Isis, the avenger of his father. Horus the Child, Heru-pa-khered, whom the Greeks called Harpocrates, was the infant with a finger to his lips and the sidelock of youth.

Ra-Horakhty, "Ra who is Horus of the two horizons", was the sun as a falcon rising and setting. Horus of Behdet, the god of Edfu, was the winged sun disc carved above countless temple doors. Over time these figures drew together, and by the late periods most texts treat them as faces of one god. You do not have to sort them perfectly. But it helps to know that the falcon over the horizon and the child on Isis's lap are both called Horus.

sections.heading: The Horus on the throne
sections.body:
Some of the oldest royal monuments in Egypt show a falcon perched on a serekh, a rectangle showing the front of a palace with the king's name inside. This "Horus name" was the first and most important of the king's names, used from before the First Dynasty. The king did not merely worship Horus; in his office, he was Horus, the god living on earth. When he died he became Osiris, and his heir became the new Horus.

That is the heart of Horus's religion. He is the rightful heir who takes up his father's place and keeps the land in order. On the famous Narmer Palette, one of the earliest royal monuments, a falcon holds a captive by a rope while the king strikes an enemy. The image is harsh, as early kingship was. In modern practice his kingship becomes something you can actually live: taking responsibility for what is yours, and defending those who depend on you.

sections.heading: His family
sections.body:
As son of Isis, Horus is the child of Osiris and Isis, conceived after Osiris's death by Isis's magic, and born and hidden in the papyrus marshes of the Delta at a place the Greeks called Chemmis. His uncle Set had murdered his father, and Horus grew up to challenge him.

His consort was Hathor, "the house of Horus", whose name contains his. At Edfu she was his wife, and every year her image travelled upriver from Dendera to visit him. Their son was Ihy, the young god of music, or at Edfu Harsomtus, "Horus who unites the two lands". The four Sons of Horus, Imsety, Hapy, Duamutef and Qebehsenuef, guarded the organs of the dead in the canopic jars. So Horus belongs at the centre of two families: the grieving household of Osiris, and the joyful household of Hathor.

knowAndDont.known: The Horus name of the king is attested from before the First Dynasty; his falcon form, his forms as Harsiese, Harpocrates, Haroeris and Ra-Horakhty, his consort Hathor and the four Sons of Horus are well documented in temple and funerary sources.
knowAndDont.unknown: The meaning of the name Heru is uncertain. How the separate Horus gods related to one another in the earliest periods, and whether the sky falcon and the son of Isis were once wholly different gods, is debated by Egyptologists.

lessons.inPractice: Choose which form of Horus you are approaching, or say honestly that you are approaching him as one god with many faces. Choose a name (Heru, Hor or Horus) and an image: a falcon wearing the double crown, a falcon-headed man, or a wedjat eye. Find a place where you can see some sky, even a window, and plan to greet him there.
reflect: Which Horus draws you: the high falcon, the vulnerable child, the son who fights for his father, or the sun on the horizon?
What in your life is yours to take responsibility for, the way an heir takes up a throne?
further: Richard H. Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003), entries on Horus and his forms
Geraldine Pinch, Egyptian Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Goddesses, and Traditions of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2004)

practices.title: Set up his shrine
practices.instructions:
Choose a shelf or small table near a window if you can, so that his shrine looks out on the sky. Wipe it with water that has a pinch of natron, washing soda or salt dissolved in it; Egyptian ritual began with purity.

Lay a clean white or gold cloth. Set his image at the back: a falcon in the double crown, a falcon-headed Horus, or a wedjat eye you have drawn yourself. In front, place a bowl for water, a dish for bread, an incense burner on a heatproof tile, and a gold, white or red candle. Add lapis lazuli or carnelian, a picture of the winged disc, or a sprig of papyrus or a lotus picture for the marshes where he was hidden.

Egyptian shrines were closed when the god was not being served. Cover the image with a cloth between visits if you can, and uncover it when you come.
practices.prompt: What did you choose for his shrine, and which form of Horus does it show?

rite.title: Introduction to Horus
rite.summary: A short first visit, by morning light if you can: purify, open the shrine, greet him by his names, offer water, bread and incense, and tell him why you have come.

ingredients.name: An offering bowl of fresh, cool water
A pinch of natron, washing soda or salt in a cup of water, for washing
An incense burner on a heatproof tile

rite.preparation: Wash your hands and face and rinse your mouth with the natron or salt water, spitting it out. Put on clean clothes. Have the shrine clean and covered. Come in the morning if you can, when the falcon is in the sky.

steps.title: Light and purify
steps.instructions: Light the candle, then the incense. Touch a drop of the natron water to your lips and pass your hands through the smoke.
steps.spoken: I am pure. My hands are washed and my mouth is clean. I come before the falcon of the sky.

steps.title: Open the shrine
steps.instructions: Uncover his image. If you can, open a window or curtain so that the sky is in view.
steps.spoken: The doors of heaven are opened. Your face is uncovered, Heru. Awake in peace.

steps.title: Adore
steps.instructions: Raise both hands, palms toward him, at the height of your face, the Egyptian gesture of praise. Hold it while you speak.
steps.spoken: Homage to you, Heru, far above, whose eyes are the sun and the moon. Son of Aset, heir of Wesir, lord of the sky: I greet you.

steps.title: Offer
steps.instructions: Lift the water, then the bread, toward him and set them down. Hold the incense up for a moment.
steps.spoken: An offering for Heru: cool water, bread and sweet smoke. I give them freely. May they please you.

steps.title: Say why you have come
steps.instructions: Speak plainly, in your own words: your name, what drew you to him, and that you will spend a month learning before you decide anything. Then sit quietly and look at the sky, or at the light on the wall.

steps.title: Close and withdraw
steps.instructions: Thank him. Cover the shrine and snuff the candle. Step back before you turn away.
steps.spoken: Go in peace, Heru. I will come again.

rite.closing: Eat the bread later in the day; that is the reversion of offerings, and nothing is wasted. Pour the water on a plant or the earth. Write a few lines in your journal.
rite.safety: Keep candle and incense on a heatproof surface in a ventilated room, away from curtains, children and pets, and never leave them burning unattended. Keep smoke away from pet birds. Do not swallow the natron water, and never look straight at the sun.

stages.title: The Son, the Contest and the Eye
stages.intro: Three lessons: the story of Horus from the marshes to the throne; the Eye of Horus and what it meant; and Edfu, where his worship is written on the walls. Keep a short morning greeting at his shrine in between.

lessons.title: From the Marshes to the Throne
lessons.summary: His hidden childhood, the long quarrel with Set, and how the gods decided between them.

sections.heading: The child in the papyrus
sections.body:
After Set killed Osiris, Isis conceived Horus by her magic and hid him in the marsh thickets of the Delta to keep him from his uncle. The healing texts are full of this time. The child is bitten by snakes and stung by scorpions, and Isis cries out for help until Thoth comes down from the sun boat and drives the poison out. On the Metternich Stela, a magical stone of the fourth century BCE now in the Metropolitan Museum, this is told at length.

Small stelae of the child Horus standing on crocodiles and holding snakes and scorpions in his fists, called cippi, were set up in homes and temples. Water poured over their carved spells was drunk or used to wash wounds as protection against bites and stings. So the first Horus most Egyptians met was not a warrior. He was a vulnerable child who survived, and who lent that survival to every child at risk.

sections.heading: The contest for the throne
sections.body:
When Horus came of age he claimed his father's throne, and Set, who held it, refused. The Pyramid Texts already know of their struggle, and of the wounds each gave the other: Set tore out Horus's eye, and Horus injured Set's testicles, a sign that both sides lost something. The gods had to decide who was in the right.

The fullest telling is a New Kingdom story, the Contendings of Horus and Set, in Papyrus Chester Beatty I from about 1150 BCE. In it the case drags on for eighty years before a divine court that keeps changing its mind. Ra favours Set, the older and stronger; Shu and Thoth favour Horus, the rightful son. There are contests of strength, a boat race in which Horus cheats by painting a wooden boat to look like stone, and a crude episode in which Set tries to shame Horus sexually and Isis turns the trick back on him. The story is funny, coarse and sometimes cruel. It is also very human: the gods are tired, partial and slow to do justice.

sections.heading: The verdict
sections.body:
In the end the court writes to Osiris in the underworld, and Osiris answers sharply, asking why his son is being cheated when it is he who makes the barley that feeds the gods. The court gives the throne to Horus. Set is not destroyed. In the Contendings, Ra takes him up to the sky to be his companion and to thunder there, so that people fear him.

Other texts tell the ending differently. In some, the gods divide Egypt, Upper Egypt to Set and Lower Egypt to Horus, before giving it all to Horus. Throne bases show Horus and Set together binding the papyrus and the lotus around the sign for "union", the two lands tied as one. The contest ends not with one god wiped out but with each in his place: Horus ruling the ordered land, Set at the edges and in the sun boat, defending it. You will meet Set's own story more fully in his journey, if you take it.

sections.heading: What the story is about
sections.body:
Egyptians told this myth at every coronation and every funeral. When a king died, his heir became Horus and buried his father as Osiris; the contest with Set was the danger of the gap between reigns, when order could fail. So the story is about succession, loyalty to a parent, and how a young person takes up a responsibility larger than they are.

It is also about justice that is slow and not always fair, and about winning without destroying. Horus does not win because he is stronger. He wins because his claim is right, because others speak for him, and because he keeps going. Many modern devotees come to him in exactly that kind of struggle: a custody case, a long fight for a just outcome, a slow recovery.

knowAndDont.known: The marsh childhood is attested in healing texts and the Metternich Stela; the struggle with Set and the injured eye from the Pyramid Texts onward; the Contendings in Papyrus Chester Beatty I (Twentieth Dynasty); the union of the two lands by Horus and Set on royal throne bases.
knowAndDont.unknown: Whether the myth reflects real wars between early kingdoms, as nineteenth- and twentieth-century scholars proposed, is now widely doubted. Versions differed by place and period, and how seriously audiences took the comic Contendings is unknown.

lessons.inPractice: Read the Contendings of Horus and Set in a modern translation (Miriam Lichtheim’s, or Simpson’s anthology). Notice who speaks up for Horus and who does not. At his shrine this week, name one matter in your life where you are waiting for a just outcome, and ask him for the strength to keep going.
reflect: Where in your life are you still in the marshes, protected and growing, and where are you ready to claim your place?
Who has spoken up for you, the way Thoth and Shu spoke for Horus? Whom could you speak up for?
further: Miriam Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature, vol. 2: The New Kingdom (1976), for the Contendings
William Kelly Simpson (ed.), The Literature of Ancient Egypt (3rd edn, 2003)
E. A. Wallis Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Project Gutenberg, for the Metternich Stela legends

lessons.title: The Eye That Was Made Whole
lessons.summary: The wedjat, how the Eye was torn and healed, and why every offering was called the Eye of Horus.

sections.heading: The torn eye
sections.body:
In the struggle with Set, Horus lost his eye, torn out or damaged, and in some tellings cut into pieces. In the Contendings, Set gouges out both his eyes and buries them, and they grow into lotus flowers; Hathor finds Horus weeping in the desert and heals him with gazelle's milk. In other texts it is Thoth who finds the pieces and puts the eye back together, which is one reason Thoth is lord of the moon, the eye that wanes and is made full again each month.

The healed eye was called the wedjat, "the sound one" or "the one that is whole". Its drawing joins a human eye and brow to the markings under a falcon's eye: a teardrop line and a spiral. It is one of the commonest amulets from ancient Egypt, worn by the living and laid on the dead, in faience, gold, carnelian and lapis.

sections.heading: Every offering is the Eye
sections.body:
In the Pyramid Texts, Horus gives his healed eye to his dead father Osiris, and by eating it Osiris is restored. From that came one of the deepest ideas in Egyptian ritual: every offering was called "the Eye of Horus". Bread, beer, water, linen and incense were presented with words naming them as the Eye, the thing that was lost and made whole, given in love from a son to a father.

This is worth taking home. When you give water and bread at any Egyptian shrine, you are, in the old way of speaking, giving the Eye of Horus: something damaged and restored, passed on to make another whole. Horus is not only a fighter. His most famous act is a gift.

sections.heading: Fractions and myths
sections.body:
You will often read that the six parts of the wedjat stood for the fractions 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32 and 1/64, used to measure grain. This idea was put forward in the early twentieth century, and Egyptologists now largely doubt it: the fraction signs look somewhat like parts of the eye, but the link seems to have been drawn by modern scholars, not by Egyptian scribes. It makes a good story, but not a safe fact.

Similarly, the wedjat is not the "all-seeing eye" of later Western symbolism, and has no ancient link to the eye on the back of the American dollar. Be careful with websites that blend them. The Egyptian Eye means protection, healing and wholeness restored.

sections.heading: The eye in the sky
sections.body:
Horus's two eyes were the sun and the moon. Some texts call the sun the right eye and the moon the left, the one that was injured and that waxes and wanes. The Eye of Ra, a fierce goddess who goes out from the sun, is a related but different idea, tied to Hathor and Sekhmet; texts sometimes blur the two.

For a devotee the sky becomes a daily reminder. The sun rising is his eye opening; the full moon is his eye made whole again; the waning moon is a wound that will heal. Many Kemetics greet Horus at dawn and look for him again in the full moon.

knowAndDont.known: The torn and restored eye appears in the Pyramid Texts, the Coffin Texts and the Contendings; the offering of the Eye of Horus to Osiris is central to Pyramid Text offering rituals; wedjat amulets survive in thousands from every period.
knowAndDont.unknown: The fraction reading of the wedjat is disputed and probably modern. Which eye was injured, and whether it was the sun or the moon, differs between texts. How the Eye of Horus and the Eye of Ra were related in Egyptian thought is not fully clear.

lessons.inPractice: Draw a wedjat by hand, slowly, and keep it on his shrine or where you need protection. When you offer anything at an Egyptian shrine this week, call it "the Eye of Horus" as you set it down. Watch the moon over the coming weeks and notice it waning and becoming whole.
reflect: What in you was damaged and has been, or is being, made whole?
What does it mean to you that Horus’s greatest act is giving his eye away?
further: Geraldine Pinch, Magic in Ancient Egypt (1994), on amulets and the wedjat
Carol Andrews, Amulets of Ancient Egypt (1994)
Jim Ritter, "Horus-Eye Fractions", in the Encyclopaedia of the History of Science, Technology, and Medicine in Non-Western Cultures (2008)

lessons.title: Edfu, Nekhen and the Living Falcon
lessons.summary: His great temples, the drama of his victory, the sacred falcon crowned each year, and the meeting with Hathor.

sections.heading: Nekhen, the old falcon city
sections.body:
Horus's oldest great home was Nekhen, which the Greeks called Hierakonpolis, "falcon city", in the far south of Egypt. It was one of the places where the Egyptian state began, before 3000 BCE, and the Narmer Palette was found in its temple. A beautiful gold falcon head, with obsidian eyes, from the Sixth Dynasty, was found there too and is now in the Egyptian Museum.

The early kings of the south took Horus of Nekhen as their god, and when they united the land, he became the god of all kingship. Recent excavations at Hierakonpolis have uncovered some of the earliest temple buildings known in Egypt.

sections.heading: The temple of Edfu
sections.body:
His best preserved temple is at Edfu, ancient Behdet, between Luxor and Aswan. It was built between 237 and 57 BCE under the Ptolemies, on the site of older temples, and it is the most complete temple surviving from ancient Egypt. Two great granite falcons stand at the gateway. Its walls are covered with texts: rituals, festival calendars, the building's own history and long myths of Horus.

One of these, the Legend of the Winged Disc, tells how Horus of Behdet flew up as a sun disc with outspread wings to fight the enemies of Ra, and how Thoth ordered that the winged disc be set over every temple door to protect it. Another, often called the Triumph of Horus, is a sacred drama in which Horus harpoons Set in the form of a hippopotamus, in ten thrusts, while Isis encourages him. It was probably performed each year at the temple's sacred lake.

sections.heading: The sacred falcon
sections.body:
Every year at Edfu, at the start of the second season, a living falcon was chosen from the birds raised at the temple and crowned as the god's living image, in a ceremony called the Coronation of the Sacred Falcon. The bird was shown at a window to the people, offered to, and installed for the year as Horus on earth, just as the king was.

As at the other great animal cults, there was also a darker side: thousands of falcons were mummified and buried as offerings by pilgrims. A modern devotee can hold that as history, and answer it with respect for living birds. Falcons are protected wild animals. Watch them in the wild, support a bird of prey rescue or conservation group, and leave feathers and nests where they are.

sections.heading: The Beautiful Meeting
sections.body:
The most joyful festival of Horus at Edfu was the Feast of the Beautiful Meeting. Each summer, in the third month of the harvest season, the image of Hathor left her temple at Dendera and sailed more than 150 kilometres upriver to visit Horus at Edfu, stopping at towns along the way. At Edfu the two gods spent about two weeks together, with processions, offerings at the necropolis to the ancestral gods, and great public feasting, before Hathor sailed home.

It was a marriage festival, and in the texts it is also a festival of victory over enemies and of renewal. It shows a side of Horus that is easy to forget: the husband and host, at the centre of a feast, music and wine, not only the avenger.

knowAndDont.known: Edfu’s building dates and inscriptions, the Legend of the Winged Disc, the Triumph of Horus drama, the Coronation of the Sacred Falcon and the Feast of the Beautiful Meeting are all recorded on the temple walls. Hierakonpolis, the Narmer Palette and the gold falcon head are excavated.
knowAndDont.unknown: How exactly the Edfu drama was staged, and how widely the festivals were kept outside Edfu and Dendera, is uncertain. The Edfu texts are Ptolemaic and may not reflect earlier practice. Exact festival dates in our calendar depend on how the Egyptian year is lined up with ours.

lessons.inPractice: Look at photographs of Edfu, especially the granite falcons and the winged disc over the doorways. Draw or print a winged disc for the top of his shrine. If you can, spend an hour this month watching birds of prey in the wild, or give to a raptor rescue. Note the Beautiful Meeting in your calendar for the summer.
reflect: What would it mean to have a winged disc over your own door?
How do you hold the history of animal offerings alongside your devotion?
further: Barbara Watterson, The House of Horus at Edfu: Ritual in an Ancient Egyptian Temple (1998)
H. W. Fairman, The Triumph of Horus: An Ancient Egyptian Sacred Drama (1974)
E. A. Wallis Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Project Gutenberg, for the Legend of Horus of Behutet and the Winged Disk

practices.title: Morning water and the sky
practices.instructions: Each morning, wash your hands and face, uncover his shrine, pour fresh water into his bowl, raise your hands, and say a line of praise. Then look at the sky for one minute, from a window or outside. Pour yesterday’s water on a plant. Cover the shrine.
practices.prompt: One line: what was the sky like this morning, and what was on your mind?

stages.title: Ten Mornings Under the Sky
stages.intro: For ten mornings, one Egyptian ten-day week, you greet Horus at his shrine and under the open sky, with an offering and a theme. Read the lesson on honouring him today before you begin.

lessons.title: Horus Today: Practice, Days and Care
lessons.summary: Modern communities, how to offer, his days through the year, and the sensitive points.

sections.heading: Who honours him now
sections.body:
Kemetic religion, the modern revival of Egyptian religion, honours Horus as one of its great gods. Reconstructionists build their practice from temple texts like those at Edfu and keep his birthday and festivals. Kemetic Orthodoxy, a temple founded in 1988 by Tamara Siuda and based in the United States, honours him in its festival calendar; its members follow that temple's own customs. Many Kemetics practise independently.

Outside Kemetic religion, eclectic Pagans and witches often call on Horus for protection, courage and victory, and sometimes draw on the wedjat as a protective sign. Thelemites honour a Horus of their own, Ra-Hoor-Khuit, within Aleister Crowley's modern system. Each of these is its own practice; be honest about which you are keeping.

sections.heading: What to offer and how
sections.body:
The offerings of the formula itself are his: bread and beer, cool water, incense, linen. Frankincense, myrrh and cedar suit him. Many devotees also offer a wedjat drawn by hand, or a feather from a farmed or moulted domestic bird (never a wild bird of prey). Name each thing as you give it, and remember that every offering is "the Eye of Horus".

Use the Egyptian shape: purify, open, adore, offer, sit, close, and then the reversion of offerings, eating or sharing the bread afterwards. In his spirit, actions count as offerings too: standing up for someone treated unfairly, keeping a promise to a parent or child, finishing a hard task you have taken on.

sections.heading: His days
sections.body:
His birthday, as Horus the Elder, is the second of the five epagomenal days, the days "upon the year" before Wep Ronpet, the new year. Wep Ronpet itself, when the order of the world is renewed and kingship with it, suits him well. At Edfu the Coronation of the Sacred Falcon fell at the start of the second season, Peret, and the Feast of the Beautiful Meeting with Hathor in the third month of the harvest season, Shemu. The Khoiak mysteries of Osiris end with the djed pillar raised and Horus crowned as his father's heir.

Modern Kemetic calendars line up these days differently, depending on how they fix the new year. Choose one calendar, note your days, and keep a few well.

sections.heading: Sensitive points
sections.body:
Horus is a god of victory, and that can be misused. He is not a god for revenge on people who have hurt you, or for curses. His fight was for a rightful place and for his father's honour, settled in the end by a court; in your life that means justice through fair means, not harm. If you are in a real conflict, use the real-world help you need, from lawyers to friends to mediators, and bring the strength you ask for into those channels.

Be careful with heritage. Egyptian religion belongs first to Egypt and to Africa, and many people of African descent find in it a source of pride; treat it with respect, not as a costume. And be careful with blended symbolism: the wedjat is not the eye of Providence, and the Aeon of Horus is not ancient.

knowAndDont.known: Kemetic Orthodoxy and Thelema are documented modern movements. The epagomenal birthdays, the Edfu festivals and the offering formula are well attested in Egyptian sources.
knowAndDont.unknown: There is no single modern Kemetic calendar, and ancient dates drifted against the seasons because the civil year had no leap day. How ordinary Egyptians, as opposed to priests and kings, approached Horus in daily life is less well known, apart from the protective cippi and amulets.

lessons.inPractice: Fix your offering habit: water most mornings, bread and beer or another drink weekly, a fuller offering on his days. Choose one act of courage or protection to offer him this month. Put his birthday and the Beautiful Meeting in your calendar.
reflect: What would it look like to ask Horus for strength without asking for revenge?
Whom do you protect, and who protects you?
further: Richard J. Reidy, Eternal Egypt: Ancient Rituals for the Modern World (2010)
Emily Teeter, Religion and Ritual in Ancient Egypt (2011)

practices.title: Ten mornings with Horus
practices.instructions:
Each morning: wash your hands and face, uncover the shrine, light the candle and incense, raise your hands and greet him. Give water and bread, saying "the Eye of Horus, for you". Then go to a window or outside and look at the sky for a few minutes with the morning's theme. Come back, write a few lines, cover the shrine and snuff the flame. Eat the bread later.

Morning 1: the falcon far above. Morning 2: the child in the marshes; what in you is still growing? Morning 3: Isis who hid him; who has protected you? Morning 4: the claim; what is rightfully yours to take up? Morning 5: the long court; a justice you are waiting for. Morning 6: the torn eye; a wound you carry. Morning 7: the Eye made whole; what has healed. Morning 8: the gift to Osiris; something you can give to restore another. Morning 9: the Beautiful Meeting; the people you love and feast with. Morning 10: the winged disc over the door; what you will protect.

If a morning is missed, carry on from where you left off. A battery candle is a fine alternative to a flame.
practices.prompt: What did this morning’s theme bring up? What did you notice in the sky?

stages.title: The Court of the Gods
stages.intro: Take a few days with only the morning water. Read your journal from the beginning, as the gods weighed the claims before them: patiently and fairly. Dedication is one good outcome; so is waiting, stopping, or finding that another god, perhaps Isis, Hathor or Ra, is the one calling you.

practices.title: Hear the case
practices.instructions: Read your journal from the first entry in one sitting. Write down, on one side of a page, what draws you to a lasting bond with Horus, and on the other what gives you pause. Then answer the questions below.
practices.prompt: If you imagine a year of greeting him each morning, what do you feel?

questions: Are you drawn to Horus himself, or mainly to strength and victory in a struggle you are facing now? Both are honest, but they may call for different choices.
Which Horus is yours: the sky falcon, the son of Isis, the child, the sun of the horizons? Can you name him at his shrine?
Can you keep a simple practice (morning water, his days, acts of protection and fairness) through an ordinary year?
Would a Kemetic community, with its own rites and teaching, serve you better than a self-dedication, at least for now?
If you decide to wait or stop, can you thank him, give a last offering and close the shrine with a clear heart? That is a good ending too.

stages.title: The Dedication
stages.intro: If you choose to go on, this is your self-dedication to Horus: a promise you write and speak yourself. It is not an initiation into Kemetic Orthodoxy or any other group, and it does not replace one. A clear morning is best; his birthday on the second epagomenal day, Wep Ronpet, or the time of the Beautiful Meeting are all fitting.

rite.title: Self-Dedication to Horus
rite.summary: A full morning rite in the Egyptian shape: purification, opening, adoration, the offering of the Eye, the vow, the drawing of the wedjat, the reversion and closing.

ingredients.name: An offering bowl of fresh water
Natron, washing soda or salt in a cup of water, for washing
Bread, and beer or another drink
Frankincense or myrrh and an incense burner
A gold, white or red candle
Paper and a pen, or red or black ink, for drawing the wedjat
Lapis lazuli or carnelian to keep on the shrine

rite.preparation:
During the day before, write your vow. Keep it short and keepable: what you will do (for example, morning water, his days kept, one act of protection or fairness each week), for how long (a year and a day is common), and what you hope for. Do not promise what you cannot give.

On the morning, bathe or shower, rinse your mouth with natron or salt water, and dress in clean, preferably white clothes. Clean the shrine and set everything out, with his image covered. Open a window or curtain toward the sky if you can.

steps.title: Purify
steps.instructions: Light the candle and the incense. Wash your hands in the natron water, touch it to your lips, and pass your hands through the smoke.
steps.spoken: I am pure, I am pure. I have washed, I have passed through the smoke. I come to Heru with clean hands and a clean mouth.

steps.title: Open the shrine
steps.instructions: Uncover his image. Look for a moment at the sky.
steps.spoken: The doors of heaven are opened. Your face is uncovered, Heru, falcon far above. Awake in peace.

steps.title: Adore
steps.instructions: Raise both hands, palms toward him, and speak the praise slowly. Add titles or words of your own if you like.
steps.spoken: Homage to you, Heru, lord of the sky, whose eyes are the sun and the moon. Child of the marshes, son of Aset, heir of Wesir, husband of Hathor, winged disc over the door. You who claimed what was yours by right, who lost your eye and gave it whole: I praise you.

steps.title: The offering of the Eye
steps.instructions: Lift the water, the bread and the drink toward him and set them down, naming each one.
steps.spoken: An offering for Heru: water, bread and drink, sweet incense, every good and pure thing. Take the Eye of Horus, made whole. May it please you.

steps.title: Speak your vow
steps.instructions: Stand and read your written vow aloud, slowly and clearly. Sign and date it.
steps.spoken: This is my word, given freely and in truth. I will keep it as well as I am able. Hear me, Heru.

steps.title: Draw the wedjat
steps.instructions: Draw a wedjat eye slowly and carefully, on your vow or on a separate piece of paper. As you draw each line, think of something in you that you want to keep whole.
steps.spoken: The Eye is whole, the Eye is sound. Let what is mine be kept whole under your wings.

steps.title: Sit with him
steps.instructions: Sit in silence before him, with the sky in view if you can. Do not hunt for signs; simply be present.

steps.title: Reversion and closing
steps.instructions: Thank him. Eat a piece of the bread. Lay the vow and the wedjat at the foot of his image. Cover the shrine and snuff the candle. Step back before you turn away.
steps.spoken: What you have received, I share. Go in peace, Heru, and come in peace. I am yours, and I will return.

rite.closing: Pour the water on the earth. Keep the wedjat on his shrine, or carry a copy with you. Record the rite in your journal, and reread your vow at each full moon, when his eye is whole.
rite.safety: Keep flame and incense on heatproof surfaces in a ventilated room, away from curtains, children, pets and especially pet birds, and never leave them burning unattended. Do not drink alcohol if you should not; water and juice are fine offerings. Never look directly at the sun.

stages.title: Under His Wings
stages.intro: After the dedication comes the steady part: water each morning, his days kept through the year, acts of courage and fairness offered in his name, and a yearly renewal of your vow.

practices.title: Morning water
practices.instructions: Most mornings, give fresh water, raise your hands and say a line of praise. Look at the sky for a moment. On busy days, a greeting from the window is enough.

practices.title: A weekly offering and act
practices.instructions: Once a week (or once in every ten days, the Egyptian week), give bread and a drink with incense, eat the bread afterwards, and offer him one act of protection, fairness or courage you did that week.
practices.prompt: What did you offer him this week, in act as well as in bread?

practices.title: His holy days
practices.instructions:
Keep his birthday on the second epagomenal day, with a fuller offering and a newly drawn wedjat. Keep Wep Ronpet, the new year, as the renewal of order. In summer, keep the Beautiful Meeting with music, a shared meal and an offering for Hathor beside his. At the end of Khoiak, when the djed is raised, honour Horus crowned as his father's heir.

Use the calendar you have chosen, and keep it from year to year.
practices.prompt: How did you keep the day, and what did it mean this year?

practices.title: Yearly rededication
practices.instructions: On the anniversary of your dedication, read the year’s journal, write a new vow, and repeat the dedication rite. Change the promise honestly: more if you can give more, less if life is harder. If you are ending the dedication, thank him, give a last offering and close the shrine with care.
practices.prompt: What has a year under his wings made stronger in you?
